submission.natural_language_explanation: Broad head: it rests on the text's first token (strength near 0) and is active (about 0.4-0.75 x max, up to 1.0 in citation or list markup) when a coordinator or list separator (' and', ' or', ' but', a list ',', '][') comes right after a noun, name, number or adjective item that is NOT the text's first token, because from there it attends with weight near 1 to that item; the word right after such a coordinator ('the', 'a') is often active too, so predict ordinary prose of 6+ tokens that contains 'X and Y' active, and other prose mixed (prepositions after a noun such as ' near', ' with', ' into' often cross 0.25 x max; sentence-final '.' and phrase-final nouns stay near 0). Predict INACTIVE (below 0.25 x max) when the only item before the coordinator is the text's first token, because then the attended item is the resting token: bare pairs such as 'bread and butter', 'salt and pepper', 'gold, silver', 'cats and dogs.', 'Tom and Mary', and texts with no coordinator at all of 3 tokens or fewer.

rival_explanations: Narrower (the earlier VERIFIED reading): the separator after the FIRST item of any run stays near 0 and only separators after the second or later item fire, so 'My cats and dogs' and 'The doctor checked her heart and lungs.' (one-item-before 'and' in mid-text) would be predicted inactive.

Broader: the head fires at any function word (coordinator or preposition such as ' near', ' with', ' into', ' on') that follows a content noun or adjective not at the text start, with coordinators not special, so prepositional prose like 'He met Tom near Mary at the station.' would be as reliably active as coordinated prose.
